title: YOUR BLOCKCHAIN HAS A MEMORY
subtitle: THE TRANSACTION YOU MADE FIVE YEARS AGO IS STILL TALKING.

blocks.text: A PUBLIC TRANSACTION DOES NOT BECOME PRIVATE WHEN YOU FORGET ABOUT IT.
THE LEDGER KEEPS RECEIPTS.

A public blockchain is not merely a payment rail. It is a durable transaction history. Addresses, amounts and transaction relationships can remain available long after the people who created them have moved on.

The dangerous assumption is that an address is harmless because nobody knows who controls it today. Attribution can happen later. Once an address or cluster becomes associated with a person, company, exchange or service, old transactions can acquire new context.
THE DATA CAN BE OLD. THE IDENTIFICATION CAN BE NEW.
TODAY'S ANONYMOUS ADDRESS CAN BECOME TOMORROW'S LABEL

Public ledgers allow observers to revisit historical activity with new information. An address posted publicly, disclosed to a counterparty, associated with an exchange account or connected through later wallet behavior can become a starting point for looking backward through the graph.

That does not mean every inference is correct. Blockchain analysis frequently relies on heuristics, and heuristics have failure modes. But permanence gives analysts something unusually valuable: the ability to rerun better tools and richer datasets against history that never disappeared.
THE GRAPH ACCUMULATES CONTEXT

One transaction may reveal little by itself. Repeated transactions can reveal patterns: recurring counterparties, consolidation behavior, change patterns, timing, payment sizes and interactions with already-labeled services. The graph becomes more informative as context accumulates.

Bitcoin privacy documentation has long described address reuse, common-input ownership and change detection as sources of linkability. Even proposals such as Payjoin explicitly discuss disrupting transaction heuristics because ordinary transaction structure can leak wallet information.
PRIVACY HAS A TIME DIMENSION

Privacy is usually discussed as a question about what an observer can learn right now. Public blockchains add another question: what might an observer learn later after acquiring information they do not possess today?
YOU ARE NOT ONLY PUBLISHING TO TODAY'S ANALYST. YOU ARE PUBLISHING TO TOMORROW'S DATASET.
WHAT SHIELDING CHANGES

Zcash takes a different approach for shielded activity. In a fully shielded transfer, protected sender and recipient information and the transferred amount are not exposed as ordinary public payment data. The blockchain still records the transaction and the cryptographic objects required for consensus, but it does not publish the same readable payment graph.
That distinction matters over time. Cryptographically protected payment details are not sitting in plaintext waiting for a future label to make the historical graph easier to interpret.
SHIELDED DOES NOT ERASE EVERYTHING

The privacy boundary still matters. Transparent interactions, information disclosed to exchanges or counterparties, transaction timing, network observations and metadata revealed outside the shielded protocol can create clues. Zcash documentation explicitly warns users about transaction metadata and network-layer correlation.
Privacy technology can reduce what the ledger permanently exposes. It cannot retract information you voluntarily publish somewhere else.
THE DIFFERENCE IN ONE LINE.
YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT TOMORROW'S DATA WILL REVEAL ABOUT YESTERDAY'S TRANSACTIONS.
